what: Mirum Pharmaceuticals sells medicines for rare liver diseases. Its main product, Livmarli, treats the relentless itching caused by Alagille syndrome and by progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, both rare genetic cholestatic conditions in children. It also sells a group of established bile acid medicines acquired from another company.
customers: Paediatric hepatologists and specialist liver centres, a small and well-defined prescriber base, with the cost met by insurers and national health systems.
money: Oral medicine for cholestatic pruritus in Alagille syndrome and PFIC, sold in the US and Europe.
Cholbam, Chenodal and related established treatments for rare bile acid disorders.
moat: Rare disease commercial economics are unusually favourable: the patients are concentrated at a handful of specialist centres, so a small sales force can reach essentially the whole market, and once a child is stabilised on a medicine that stops intractable itching, nobody changes it. Orphan drug exclusivity and the sheer difficulty of running trials in tiny paediatric populations keep competitors away.
risks: The trailing twelve months show a net loss of about $903.9M against only $23.4M of loss in the last reported fiscal year, so the period contains a charge far larger than the operating business. Free cash flow of roughly negative $273.9M is much smaller than the reported loss, which confirms most of it was non-cash.
The shares trade at about 9.3 times sales, which requires the product portfolio to keep growing at the current rate.
Revenue depends heavily on one medicine in two very rare indications, so the addressable patient count is finite and reaching most of it means growth must come from new indications or new products.
Rare disease pricing attracts scrutiny from insurers and from governments, and reimbursement negotiations in Europe have been slower than in the US.
Thirteen analysts average a $157.71 target against $95.51, a 65% gap that reflects very different views on the pipeline rather than a settled valuation.
opportunities: Revenue growth has been exceptional, from $19.1M in 2021 to $521.3M in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $670.8M.
Cash of $383.3M against almost no debt, at $9.7M, is a strong position for a company of this size.
Diagnosis rates in rare cholestatic liver disease are improving, which expands the treated population without any change in the medicine.
The acquired bile acid products add immediate revenue and use the same specialist sales force, so the incremental cost of selling them is small.
A profitable rare disease commercial platform is a frequent acquisition target for larger pharmaceutical companies.
watch: Livmarli revenue by quarter and progress in new indications. The commercial base is proved; whether the addressable population widens is what determines if this is a $700M business or a $2B one.
view: Set the trailing loss aside first, because it will mislead anyone who reads it literally. Mirum shows $904 million of net loss over the trailing twelve months against a $23 million loss in the last full fiscal year, while cash outflow was only $274 million. A loss four times larger than the cash it consumed is an accounting charge, not a business collapse — in this sector it is almost always an acquisition-related or intangible write-off. The operating company underneath grew revenue from $19 million to over $670 million in four years. That is the figure that describes what Mirum actually is.

What it is, is a well-executed rare disease commercial platform, and those are better businesses than their size suggests. The patients with Alagille syndrome and PFIC are treated at a limited number of specialist paediatric liver centres, which means a modest sales force can cover essentially the entire market — the brutal commercial economics of primary care simply do not apply. The medicine treats an itch so severe that children scratch themselves raw and some end up transplanted, so adherence is not a problem and nobody experiments with switching. Orphan exclusivity and the near-impossibility of running a competing paediatric trial in a population this small keep the field clear. Add the acquired bile acid products, sold by the same representatives at almost no incremental cost, and the operating leverage is real.

The limit on all of this is arithmetic. A finite number of children have these diseases. Mirum has already captured a substantial share of the diagnosed population, which is why the argument has shifted to improving diagnosis rates and to new indications. Those are legitimate growth sources and they are also the entire gap between the $95 share price and the $158 analyst average. You are not being asked to judge whether the current products work; they plainly do. You are being asked whether the addressable population widens from here, which is a pipeline and diagnosis question dressed up as a commercial one.

At 9.3 times sales with $383 million of cash and essentially no debt, the price assumes the answer is yes. I would call that a fair price for a proven platform with an unproven extension, and I would note that this profile — profitable specialist sales force, rare disease franchise, clean balance sheet — is precisely what large pharmaceutical companies buy when they need revenue. That optionality is part of what you own. Track Livmarli revenue quarter by quarter against the estimated diagnosed population, because the moment that curve flattens, the growth has to come from the pipeline and the stock will be repriced on pipeline terms.
bull: Diagnosis rates keep rising and new indications widen the treated population, turning a proven rare disease platform into a much larger revenue base — or an acquisition target.
bear: Penetration of a finite patient population plateaus, the pipeline disappoints, and 9.3 times sales meets a business that has already captured most of its market.
